headline: Connecticut sends $2 million in math tutoring grants to 42 education agencies
dek: The state says the new awards will extend intensive, curriculum-linked math support into grades 6 through 10 during the 2026-27 school year.
body: Connecticut is directing $2 million to 42 local education agencies for high-dosage mathematics tutoring, a state investment that expands the program into grades 6 through 10 during the 2026-27 school year. The [Connecticut State Department of Education](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/press-room/press-releases/2026/connecticut-state-department-of-education-awards-%242-million-in-high-dosage-tutoring-grants) announced the awards on Oct. 5 after receiving 70 applications. The department said the full amount available through the competitive grant round will go to local agencies.

The awards reach districts and regional or charter-school organizations across the state. The published list includes Bridgeport, Danbury, Hartford, Stamford and Waterbury, each receiving $50,000, along with smaller awards for places such as Middletown, Preston, Regional School District 11 and Southington. The list also includes education service organizations such as ACES and EASTCONN. Those awards do not by themselves establish how many students each agency will serve; local plans and implementation details will determine the reach of the tutoring.

Connecticut initially used nearly $11.5 million in federal American Rescue Plan Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief funding to launch high-dosage tutoring in mathematics for students in grades 6 through 9. The new round is funded through the state’s fiscal 2027 budget and moves the upper grade boundary to 10. The [department’s program overview](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/covid19/acceleratect/high-dosage-tutoring) describes the change as a continuation of the earlier effort rather than a separate, unrelated initiative.

The state’s definition of high-dosage tutoring is more specific than a conventional after-school homework session. The model calls for tutoring multiple times a week, one-on-one or small-group instruction, a consistent tutor, lessons aligned with grade-level mathematics and integration into the school day when possible. The [competitive grant notice](https://portal.ct.gov/sde/rfp/request-for-proposals/2026-rfps) says the grants are intended to help agencies use those evidence-based guidelines to accelerate learning and address gaps that worsened during the pandemic.

The department says the earlier program produced measurable gains for participating students, but that figure is a state-reported program result rather than an independent evaluation of the new awards. On Smarter Balanced assessments, CSDE says students who received the tutoring saw proficiency rates rise by about 9 percentage points and mathematics achievement increase by about 9 scale-score points. The announcement does not say that every district, grade or student will experience the same result, and the new grants will need to be tracked as local programs get underway.

The new awards also put a statewide policy choice into practice. Connecticut lawmakers created a high-dosage tutoring matching-grant program in the 2026 session, and the department’s current round uses that authorization to keep targeted math support in place after the one-time federal relief that helped start the program. That matters for districts that built tutoring around the earlier funding but still face uneven mathematics performance and limited time during the regular school day.

For families, the immediate question is not how to apply for a state check. The money is going to school systems and other local education agencies, which will decide how to schedule tutoring, identify students and hire or train tutors within the state’s guidelines. The Oct. 5 announcement names the awardees but does not publish a single statewide enrollment date or a common family application. Parents and caregivers will therefore need to watch their district or school communications for details about eligibility, timing and whether tutoring will be offered during the school day, an intervention period or another scheduled block.

The next test will be implementation. Connecticut has committed the money and identified the agencies, but the public release leaves several operational questions open, including how many students will participate, how districts will report attendance and whether the gains cited from the earlier program will hold across the expanded grades. The new grants give schools another tool for mathematics recovery; their regional impact will become clearer as agencies turn the awards into recurring small-group instruction and publish results from the 2026-27 school year.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Connecticut awards $2 million for high-dosage math tutoring
seoDescription: Connecticut awarded $2 million in 2026-27 high-dosage math tutoring grants to 42 local education agencies serving grades 6 through 10.
